issues.body: The module reduces the check to sigma = sum_i lambda_i(delta'_i - alpha*delta_i) and says Delta_v=0 means "not changing the answer." That is valid only for one checked product. malicious_secure_equal_batch checks a random linear combination, so the actual shifts also carry per-product challenge factors chi_j. Multiple nonzero product shifts can have sum_j chi_j Delta_v,j=0 while changing individual opened products and equality bits. Such cancellation should be unlikely when deviations are fixed before an unpredictable challenge, but that is a separate 1/p/Fiat-Shamir argument (and grinding residual), not a consequence of alpha secrecy. The new <=t tests exercise only one product at a time, so they do not pin the load-bearing all-pairs single-sigma claim.
issues.fix_hint: State the batched equation with both recombination weights and Fiat-Shamir coefficients, and separate the two failure cases: nonzero aggregate value shift requires forging against alpha, while a zero aggregate shift with nonzero per-product shifts requires a random-linear-combination collision. Give the resulting bound (including the documented Fiat-Shamir/grinding scope) without saying aggregate zero implies unchanged answers. Add a production-path batch adversarial test with at least two products and <=t-party in-resharing deviations that would alter individual verdicts if accepted, and a mutation/witness showing the test fails when challenge binding or the batch check is removed.
issues.title: The malicious-security argument omits cross-pair cancellation in the batched MAC check

verdict.summary: Round 2 is improving: the two prior findings about modeling a <=t-party attacker are substantially addressed by the new in-resharing deviation hook, the clearly separated corrupt-dealer tests, and the share-level single-product argument. One load-bearing gap remains in the advertised batched API. The proof in auth_equal.rs drops the batch challenge coefficients and incorrectly equates a zero aggregate value shift with an unchanged answer. For a batch, distinct product shifts can cancel in the random linear combination while individual equality bits change; security then depends on the Fiat-Shamir random-combination bound, not solely on secrecy of alpha. The implementation may still have the intended bound, but the stated proof and adversarial tests do not establish the public single-sigma batch claim as written.
